Memory.value: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together

vignette:
James, a 29-year-old Coast Guard officer, had always prided himself on his ability to stay calm under pressure. However, that sense of control was shattered one evening while he was walking home from a late shift. As he navigated the dimly lit streets, two men approached him, their faces obscured by hoods. In a matter of moments, they were upon him, demanding his wallet and phone. The adrenaline surged through him as he instinctively fought back, but the encounter left him sprawled on the ground, feeling the cold concrete beneath him. The last thing he remembered was the sharp pain in his side as one of the assailants struck him. After they fled, James lay there, gasping, his mind racing yet strangely detached. 

In the weeks that followed, James found himself replaying that night repeatedly, but the memories were jumbled and fragmented. He could not seem to articulate the experience; words escaped him as if they belonged to someone else’s story. He felt as if he were watching a movie, where the scenes flashed by without coherence, leaving him with a sense of emotional numbness. When he tried to talk about it with his partner, the words failed him, and he would often fall silent, feeling like a spectator to his own life. This disconnect only deepened his frustration and sense of isolation. His partner, who was eager to help, often found herself at a loss, unsure of how to reach him when he seemed so far away.

At work, the trauma haunted him in more subtle ways. The sound of a sudden noise or the sight of someone approaching him too quickly would send a chill down his spine. He found himself avoiding certain routes home and opting to take longer, well-lit paths, even if it meant extending his commute. His colleagues, noticing his withdrawal and quieter demeanor, began to comment on his change in behavior. James shrugged off their concerns, convincing himself that he just needed time to process what had happened. But deep down, he feared that his inability to share his feelings was pushing him further away from those he cared about. He often felt like he was living in a bubble, surrounded by people, yet completely disconnected from them.

Over time, this avoidance became a pattern. He stopped going out with friends and declined invitations, preferring the comfort of solitude where he could shield himself from the unpredictability of social interactions. The numbness he felt began to seep into every part of his life, and he found it increasingly hard to engage with his work and relationships. What frightened him most was the gradual realization that he was losing parts of himself—his sense of humor, his spontaneity, his connection to others. His partner’s patience was wearing thin, and he sensed her growing concern, yet he felt powerless to articulate what was happening inside him.

Now, as he sat in the therapist’s office, James grappled with his emotions and the weight of his experience. He had come to seek help not only for himself but also for the sake of his relationship. The fear of losing his partner loomed large; he could not imagine facing life alone, yet he felt so far removed from the person he used to be. He hoped that through therapy, he could finally piece together the shattered fragments of that night and reclaim the emotional connection he had lost, but a part of him wondered if he would ever be able to truly share his story.
